name: Nuremberg Violet
lede: Nuremberg violet is an old trade name for manganese violet, a purple pigment made from manganese phosphates and introduced in 1868.

sections.title: Manganese violet by another name
sections.body:
Nuremberg violet is a synonym for manganese violet, which the Dictionary of Colour says was brought in during 1868 to offer a safer substitute for the toxic cobalt violet [1]. The Pigment Compendium lists it, also spelled Nürnberg violet, among synonyms for a manganese ammonium phosphate pigment [2]. In practice, it adds, the name was probably used for one of several manganese phosphates [2]. See [[manganese-violet]]; the swatch is a mid purple close to [[violet]] and [[purple]] [3].

The name points to the German city of Nuremberg (Nürnberg), but the books consulted do not explain the choice, so its origin is undocumented here [1][2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The name is recorded as a color in the 1930 Maerz and Paul dictionary [3]. The color library files it as a purple, near [[plum]] and [[mauve]] [3]. In our archive it is found in 1 painting out of 23,781, as photographed, so the screen color is nearly absent from paint on canvas [3]. A modern violet pigment is no guarantee of the same hue in a varnished picture [3].

sections.title: Manganese violet and its rivals
sections.body: Manganese violet came late to the palette. By 1868, when it was introduced, artists already had cobalt violet and the new aniline purples such as [[mauve]], which had been on sale since 1856 [1][4]. Its appeal was safety: cobalt violet is toxic, and the manganese phosphate pigments were seen as the milder choice [1]. The Compendium says the name was probably used for one of several manganese phosphates, so the exact composition behind it is uncertain [2].
